findings.sub_question: How do production multi-agent research systems concretely aggregate subagent outputs into a single coherent report without the writer-fragmentation pathology Cognition warns about — what synthesis/handoff protocols (shared scratchpads, structured JSON schemas, judge-then-merge, single-writer-with-read-only-researchers) are documented to work, and which fail?
findings.summary:
Across primary sources from Cognition, Anthropic, LangChain, and several 2025–2026 papers, a striking convergence emerges: the synthesis pattern that reliably works in production is single-writer-with-read-only-researchers. Cognition's June 2025 essay (Yan, 'Don't Build Multi-Agents') argued that parallel writer agents fragment because actions carry implicit decisions that cannot be reconciled post-hoc; their April 2026 follow-up ('Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working') explicitly retracts the blanket prohibition but only for setups 'where multiple agents contribute intelligence to a task while writes stay single-threaded.' They report that most production-grade multi-agent setups are still limited to read-only subagents (web search, code search, Deepwiki) that 'mostly resemble tool calls rather than true multi-agent collaboration,' and that unstructured swarms remain 'mostly a distraction.' The successful shape is map-reduce-and-manage: a manager splits work, children execute in isolated contexts, the manager synthesizes and reports back.

Anthropic's 'How we built our multi-agent research system' (June 13, 2025) is the canonical production implementation of exactly this pattern. A LeadResearcher (Claude Opus 4) plans, spawns parallel Sonnet 4 subagents with structured task descriptions (each gets 'an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries'), waits synchronously for them to finish, then synthesizes — and only then a separate CitationAgent post-processes for citation attribution. The lead saves its plan to external Memory before spawning so the plan survives 200K-token truncation. Crucially, Anthropic explicitly addresses the 'game of telephone' problem with two appendix-level techniques: (1) subagents write large outputs to a filesystem and pass lightweight references back, bypassing the coordinator for high-fidelity artifacts; and (2) when context fills, agents 'spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs' via stored research plans. They beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on internal research evals but burn ~15× more tokens than chat. The Claude Opus 4.5 system card (Nov 2025) confirms this architecture in production, showing Opus-orchestrator-with-Haiku-subagents reaches 87.0% on internal multi-agent search vs. 74.8% single-agent.

LangChain's open-deep-research is the most documented open-source instantiation and explicitly cites Cognition's warning as the reason for its design. Their July 2025 blog states: 'Earlier versions of our research agent wrote sections of the final report in parallel with sub-agents. It was fast, but we faced a problem that Cognition raised: the reports were disjoint because the section-writing agents were not well coordinated. We resolved this by using multi-agent for only the research task itself, performing writing after all research was done.' The final report is generated 'in one-shot, steered by the brief and answered with the research findings.' The code (deep_researcher.py) shows the concrete protocol: subagents return Pydantic-typed ConductResearch/ResearchComplete tool calls; each subagent calls a separate compress_research node before returning to the supervisor (a citation-preserving compression step that prevents raw tool dumps from polluting orchestrator context); the supervisor aggregates `notes` (compressed strings) and only at the very end does final_report_generation run a single LLM call over the brief + concatenated notes.

Several 2025–2026 papers document complementary protocols that all converge on the same single-writer pattern with structured intermediate artifacts. ADORE (arXiv 2601.18267) introduces 'memory-locked synthesis' — generation is hard-constrained to a structured Memory Bank (Claim–Evidence Graph) with section-level admissible evidence, plus 'evidence-coverage–guided execution' that audits per-section coverage to drive targeted re-retrieval and an evidence-driven stopping rule. WebWeaver (cited by ADORE) uses outline-centric evidence structuring with section-level writing on top of a memory bank. Mind2Report (arXiv 2601.04879) uses an intent-clarification → outline → recursive search with multi-dimensional reflection (integrity/freshness/plurality) → dynamic memory keyed to outline chapters → coherent-preserved iterative synthesis with knowledge merging before reference matching. Static-DRA (arXiv 2512.03887) uses depth/breadth parameters over a Supervisor/Independent/Worker tree where workers do leaf-level search and parents recursively concatenate citations + reports. Judge-then-merge appears mainly as a *post-hoc evaluator*, not as a writer-merge mechanism: DeepResearch-ReportEval (arXiv 2510.07861) and the Deep Research Bench RACE framework score finished reports across quality/redundancy/factuality using LLM-as-judge, and Cognition reports that Devin's 'review-loop' (a clean-context reviewer reading only the final diff) catches an average of 2 bugs per PR with 58% severe — but the reviewer never writes; it only emits findings the original writer integrates. 

What fails: (a) Parallel writer swarms producing different sections concurrently (LangChain explicitly tried this and abandoned it; Cognition's Flappy Bird example; arXiv survey reports 41–86.7% production failure rates for collaborative-write multi-agent traces). (b) Passing only summaries between agents — Cognition: 'summaries lose the implicit decisions … full trace-sharing is the only thing that actually works,' which then runs into context limits. (c) Edit-apply two-model patterns where a small model rewrites based on a large model's markdown instructions — Cognition reports these fail on subtle ambiguities in the instructions and have been largely abandoned by 2025 in favor of single-model edit decisions. (d) Unstructured agent-to-agent negotiation/swarms — Cognition (2026): 'mostly a distraction'; current models lack the cross-context proactive discourse needed. (e) Naive long-context dumping of all subagent outputs into a single writer — Anthropic and Mind2Report both show this triggers context rot; the working pattern is per-section compression + structured memory + a writer that retrieves on demand from that memory rather than ingesting everything at once.

key_facts.claim: The single-writer-with-read-only-researchers pattern (one orchestrator/writer + parallel read-only investigative subagents) is the synthesis protocol Anthropic, Cognition (in their April 2026 update), and LangChain all independently converged on as the one that works in production.

Cognition's original June 2025 critique argued parallel writer subagents fail because 'actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results' — subagents working in parallel cannot see each other's implicit choices (style, schemas, edge cases) and produce incompatible artifacts that the final agent cannot reconcile.

Cognition's April 2026 follow-up explicitly confirms multi-agent works only when 'writes stay single-threaded' and additional agents 'contribute intelligence rather than actions'; they call unstructured agent-to-agent swarms 'mostly a distraction' and describe the working shape as map-reduce-and-manage.

Anthropic's production Research feature uses an orchestrator-worker pattern: a LeadResearcher (Opus 4) plans and saves the plan to external Memory before spawning, dispatches Sonnet 4 subagents with structured task descriptions (objective, output format, tool/source guidance, task boundaries), waits synchronously, synthesizes, then a separate CitationAgent post-processes citations.
Anthropic's multi-agent research system outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research eval but uses ~15× more tokens than chat (vs. ~4× for single agents).

Anthropic specifically mitigates the 'game of telephone' between subagents and coordinator by having subagents write large outputs to a filesystem (artifact system) and pass only lightweight references back to the lead — bypassing token-overhead from copying outputs through conversation history.

When context fills, Anthropic's agents 'spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs' — retrieving stored context (research plan) from memory rather than losing previous work at the context limit.

LangChain's open-deep-research explicitly tried writing report sections in parallel with subagents, hit Cognition's predicted disjointness, and refactored to use multi-agent only for the research phase with the final report 'produced in one-shot' from the brief plus aggregated findings.

Open-deep-research's concrete protocol uses Pydantic structured-output schemas (ConductResearch, ResearchComplete, ResearchQuestion, ClarifyWithUser) as the typed handoff format between supervisor and subagents, and includes a dedicated compress_research LLM call inside each subagent that compresses raw tool outputs into a clean string before returning to the supervisor — preventing raw tool dumps from polluting orchestrator context.

Read-only subagents (web search, code search, Deepwiki-style codebase context) 'mostly resemble tool calls rather than true multi-agent collaboration' and represent the dominant production-deployed multi-agent pattern as of 2026.

ADORE (arXiv 2601.18267) operationalizes 'memory-locked synthesis': report generation is hard-constrained to a structured Memory Bank (Claim–Evidence Graph) with section-level admissible evidence, ensuring claim-to-source traceability, plus evidence-coverage–guided execution that drives targeted follow-up retrieval and provides an evidence-driven stopping rule rather than a fixed iteration budget.

Mind2Report (arXiv 2601.04879) uses a dynamic memory keyed to an outline chapter tree, with multi-dimensional reflection (integrity, freshness, plurality, search-steps) gating what enters memory, then performs 'coherent-preserved iterative synthesis' that merges knowledge sharing the same source before sequential per-segment writing — explicitly to mitigate hallucinations and stay within context limits.

Judge-then-merge appears in production primarily as an evaluation/review pattern (DeepResearch-ReportEval scores quality/redundancy/factuality with LLM-as-judge; Devin Review catches ~2 bugs/PR with 58% severe) — but the reviewer does not write; it emits findings the original single writer integrates.

Cognition reports the generator-verifier (code-review) loop works best when the reviewer has a completely clean context with no shared context with the writer — because clean context evades context rot and forces the reviewer to reason backward from the artifact, but the writer still owns all writes and decides which findings to integrate.

Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.5 system card confirms the orchestrator-worker pattern in production: Opus-4.5 orchestrator with Haiku-4.5 subagents reaches 87.0% on multi-agent search vs. 74.8% single-agent Opus-4.5 — a +12.2pp improvement attributable purely to delegating search to lightweight read-only subagents while keeping orchestration single-threaded.

Static-DRA (arXiv 2512.03887) demonstrates a hierarchical Supervisor/Independent/Worker tree with user-tunable depth/breadth where parent agents simply concatenate citations and reports from children — only leaf workers do search, only the root produces final output, and breadth is reduced by 2 at each deeper level to focus depth where it matters.

Empirical production failure rates for multi-agent systems are reported at 41–86.7% across studied execution traces, with specification failures (~42%) and coordination breakdowns (~37%) the dominant categories — both extremely difficult to diagnose because the failure signal is usually a subtly wrong output rather than an exception.

Edit-apply patterns (large model outputs markdown instructions, small model rewrites file) were widely used in 2024 but found fragile because the small model misinterpreted subtle ambiguities; by 2025 the field largely consolidated edit decisions and applying into a single model action.

Anthropic's recent Multiagent Sessions API (Research Preview, ~2026) operationalizes the working pattern in protocol form: a coordinator agent's primary thread sees only condensed activity from spawned subagent threads; subagents have isolated context and tools; tool/permission events route via session_thread_id so the coordinator stays the single writer of user-facing output. Crucially the API limits delegation to one level — children cannot spawn children.

findings.sub_question: What does the 2024–2026 evaluation-methodology literature (e.g., LiveResearchBench, DeepResearch Bench, MAS evaluation critiques) say about the right way to compare single-agent vs multi-agent deep-research architectures — specifically, should comparisons normalize on tokens, dollars, wall-clock, or task-completion, and how much do reported quality gaps move under each normalization?
findings.summary:
The 2024–2026 evaluation-methodology literature converges on a strong, near-unanimous critique: comparing single-agent (SAS) and multi-agent systems (MAS) on task-completion or quality alone is misleading, because most reported MAS advantages are confounded by extra test-time compute. Kapoor et al.'s 'AI Agents That Matter' (2024, TMLR 2025) is the load-bearing source. They show simple baselines (retry, warming, escalation) match SOTA complex agents on HumanEval while costing up to ~50× less (e.g., LATS uses ~$134 of GPT-4 for substantially the same accuracy as a $2.45 'warming' loop), demonstrate joint cost–accuracy optimization (DSPy + Optuna) that cuts HotPotQA cost ~41–53% with no accuracy loss, and argue that for *model* evaluation researchers should control compute, while for *downstream* (procurement) evaluation they should report dollar cost and raw input/output token counts so users can re-price as APIs change. Subsequent work — Cemri et al.'s MAST/'Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?' (NeurIPS 2025), Mehta's CLEAR framework (2025), BAMAS (2025), and BATS (2025) — extends this into formal multi-dimensional rubrics (cost, latency, accuracy, assurance, reliability) and explicit cost-normalized accuracy (CNA = Accuracy/Cost), showing 50× cost variations for similar accuracy and that 'accuracy-optimal configurations cost 4.4–10.8× more than Pareto-efficient alternatives.'

When the normalizations are actually applied, the reported MAS quality gap moves dramatically and often disappears. The cleanest direct test is Tran & Kiela's 2026 study, which compares SAS against five MAS topologies (Sequential, Subtask-parallel, Parallel-roles, Debate, Ensemble) across Qwen3-30B, DeepSeek-R1-70B-Distill, and Gemini-2.5 Flash/Pro under *matched thinking-token budgets* of 100, 500, 1k, 2k, 5k, 10k tokens on FRAMES and MuSiQue. They find SAS matches or outperforms every MAS variant at every budget except the smallest (where neither produces useful reasoning) — formally backed by a Data Processing Inequality argument that any messages M = g(C) passed between agents lose information relative to the full context C, so a single agent with the same budget is information-theoretically guaranteed to be at least as good. They explicitly conclude that 'many reported MAS gains are better explained by compute and context effects than by inherent architectural superiority.' MAS only becomes competitive when single-agent context utilization is heavily degraded (e.g., 70% token substitution noise). Anthropic's June 2025 engineering blog effectively concedes the same point in their own data: their multi-agent Research system uses ~15× more tokens than chat (vs ~4× for a single-agent), and 'three factors explained 95% of the performance variance in BrowseComp evaluation … token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance' — i.e., most of their headline 90.2% multi-agent uplift over single-agent Claude Opus 4 is buying tokens, not architecture.

The specific deep-research benchmarks differ sharply on whether they implement these recommendations. LiveResearchBench (Wang et al., Salesforce + UW-Madison, Oct 2025) evaluates 17 systems (single-agent web, single-agent deep research, multi-agent) across six quality dimensions and is the most-cited recent comparison, but it does *not* normalize on tokens, dollars, or wall-clock — its v5 'Knowledge Gaps' section explicitly admits 'fairness across system resources' is unaddressed and lists 'cost and latency reporting' as required future work. It does, however, provide qualitative diagnostics: single-agent deep research systems (Gemini DR, OpenAI o3 DR) produce substantially longer reports than multi-agent ones, but length 'reflects citation handling as much as content,' and longer reports do not monotonically improve quality. Multi-agent systems lead the average composite (e.g., Open Deep Research with GPT-5: 73.7; Salesforce AIR: 76.5; Deerflow+: 72.9) but mainly via citation-association and presentation, not analytical depth — only Deerflow+ and Gemini Deep Research beat Open Deep Research on win-rate over depth. DeepResearch Bench (Du et al., USTC, June 2025; v2 Dec 2025) similarly omits agent-side cost from its RACE/FACT leaderboard, reporting only the per-query *judge* cost ($0.13 for Gemini-2.5 Pro). BrowseComp-Plus (Chen, Ma et al., Aug 2025; ACL 2026) is the most rigorous on this dimension: it fixes the corpus to disentangle retriever from agent, and reports per-system API cost in USD (e.g., Claude Opus 4: $2,043 for the 830-query benchmark vs Gemini 2.5 Flash: $47), search-call counts, and accuracy together — making cost-normalized comparison reproducible.

Quantitatively, the gap movement under each normalization is substantial. Under task-completion only, multi-agent systems appear to win by 5–20 points on most aggregated leaderboards. Under dollar normalization, the picture inverts in many cases: in the financial-document benchmark (Kulkarni & Kulkarni, 2025), the reflexive (multi-agent) architecture achieves the top F1 of 0.943 but at 2.3× the sequential baseline cost; the hierarchical architecture achieves 98.5% of that F1 at 60.7% of the cost; and a 'Hierarchical-Optimized' configuration recovers 89% of reflexive's accuracy gain at only 1.15× sequential cost — i.e., the apparent ~3.5 F1-point multi-agent advantage shrinks to ~1.5 points and reverses on cost-normalized accuracy. Mehta's CLEAR results show Reflexion's 74.1% efficacy is dominated by Plan-Execute's 71.9% (a 2.2-point gap shrinking to 'dominated' under joint cost) at $5.12 vs $1.24 per task. Under wall-clock / throughput normalization the picture changes again: the financial benchmark shows reflexive's p99 latency is 3.34× its p50 (vs 1.6× for sequential), and reflexive *becomes the worst* architecture above 50K docs/day because timeout-truncated correction loops eliminate its accuracy advantage; the architectural crossover where hierarchical drops below parallel occurs around 75K docs/day on a fixed cluster. Under tool-call-budget normalization (BATS, 2025), 'standard agents lack inherent budget awareness' and saturate at ~12% accuracy on BrowseComp regardless of additional budget; explicit budget-aware sequential and parallel scaling (with the Budget Tracker plug-in) traces a much steeper Pareto curve and pushes the cost–performance frontier substantially. 

Methodological cautions cluster around three pitfalls noted by Tran & Kiela and others: (1) API-reported token counts can be unreliable as effective-compute proxies — for Gemini-2.5, the API's `thoughts_token_count` is up to 4.7× the visible-thought token count, and visible thought plateaus at ~350 tokens regardless of requested budget, so 'matched budget' must be defined on the *requested* budget; (2) sequential MAS naturally inflates visible-thought-token counts simply by concatenating k agent calls, biasing token-based comparisons; (3) dollar costs change overnight as APIs reprice, so Kapoor et al. recommend reporting raw input/output token counts and exposing recalculable cost so evaluations remain valid over time. The community recommendation that emerges across these sources is therefore *multi-axis Pareto reporting*: every leaderboard should publish accuracy alongside (a) input/output token counts, (b) tool-call counts, (c) dollar cost at a stated date, and (d) wall-clock p50/p95/p99, and rankings should be presented as Pareto frontiers rather than single numbers. Deep-research-specific benchmarks (LiveResearchBench, DeepResearch Bench) have not yet adopted this; BrowseComp-Plus and the agentic-benchmark critique literature are leading practice.

key_facts.claim: The seminal critique by Kapoor, Stroebl, Siegel, Nadgir & Narayanan (Princeton, 2024; published in TMLR 2025) argues that AI agent evaluations must be cost-controlled because simple baselines like Retry, Warming, and Escalation match or beat SOTA complex agents (LDB, LATS, Reflexion) on HumanEval at fraction of the cost, with LATS-GPT4 costing ~$134.50 per run vs warming-GPT4 at $2.45 for indistinguishable accuracy — roughly a 55× cost gap.

Kapoor et al. specifically distinguish 'model evaluation' (which should normalize compute, e.g., active parameters or training FLOPs) from 'downstream evaluation' (which should report dollar cost and raw input/output token counts), and argue proxies like Mistral's 'active parameters' are misleading for procurement decisions because Mixtral 8x7B costs 2× Llama-2-13B on Anyscale despite similar active-parameter counts.

Tran & Kiela (Stanford, 2026) present an information-theoretic argument grounded in the Data Processing Inequality: under fixed thinking-token budgets and perfect context utilization, single-agent systems (SAS) are at least as good as multi-agent systems (MAS) because messages M=g(C) cannot increase mutual information with the answer Y beyond what the full context C provides.

In controlled experiments across Qwen3-30B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, and Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro, with 5 MAS architectures (Sequential, Subtask-parallel, Parallel-roles, Debate, Ensemble) on FRAMES and MuSiQue 4-hop at matched thinking-token budgets of 100/500/1k/2k/5k/10k, SAS consistently matches or outperforms MAS at every non-trivial budget — overturning typical leaderboard results.

Anthropic's own engineering report (June 2025) on their multi-agent Research system concedes that '95% of performance variance on BrowseComp' across their configurations is explained by three factors, with 'token usage by itself explain[ing] 80% of the variance,' implying most apparent multi-agent gains buy tokens rather than architectural superiority.

Anthropic reports that their multi-agent Research system using Claude Opus 4 (lead) + Sonnet 4 (subagents) outperforms single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on internal research evals, but uses approximately 4× more tokens than chat for single-agent and approximately 15× more tokens than chat for multi-agent, requiring tasks where the value justifies the cost.

Cemri et al. (Berkeley, NeurIPS 2025 'Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?' / MAST) find that 'despite enthusiasm for MAS, their performance gains on popular benchmarks are often minimal compared to single-agent frameworks or even simple baselines such as best-of-N sampling,' citing Kapoor et al. 2024 as direct support.

Cemri et al. catalog 14 distinct MAS failure modes in 3 categories (Specification & System Design, Inter-Agent Misalignment, Task Verification) across 150+ traces from 5 MAS frameworks, and find that 'best-effort' tactical interventions (improved prompts, topology changes) yield only ~14% improvement on ChatDev — far short of structural fixes that would be needed.

LiveResearchBench (Wang et al., Salesforce + UW-Madison, arXiv 2510.14240, October 2025) evaluates 17 deep-research systems across single-agent-with-search, single-agent deep research, and multi-agent deep research categories using six DeepEval quality dimensions, but does NOT normalize on tokens, dollars, or wall-clock; the v5 (April 2026) 'Knowledge Gaps' section explicitly lists 'fairness across system resources' and 'cost and latency reporting' as unresolved.

LiveResearchBench observes that single-agent deep-research systems (e.g., Gemini Deep Research, OpenAI o3 Deep Research) produce substantially longer reports than multi-agent systems, but report length 'reflects citation handling as much as content' and 'longer reports do not necessarily translate into higher quality,' and characterizes most current systems as 'deep searchers, not deep researchers.'

DeepResearch Bench (Du et al., USTC + Metastone, arXiv 2506.11763, June 2025) uses RACE (reference-based adaptive criteria) and FACT (citation accuracy + effective citation count) and reports judge cost (Gemini-2.5-Pro: $0.13/query) but does NOT report system-side dollar cost, tokens, or wall-clock; rankings are based on quality scores alone.

DeepResearch Bench II (Li, Du, et al., December 2025) uses 9,430 fine-grained binary rubrics across 132 expert-derived tasks and finds even the best system (OpenAI o3 Deep Research) satisfies fewer than 50% of rubrics — a substantial gap to human experts — but again does not include cost or token normalization in its main comparison.

BrowseComp-Plus (Chen, Ma et al., University of Waterloo, August 2025) explicitly designs for fair, transparent evaluation by fixing the corpus to decouple retriever from LLM agent and reports per-system API costs in USD: e.g., Claude Opus 4 on the 830-query benchmark costs $2,043.95 with BM25 vs Gemini-2.5-Flash at $47.32, while accuracy ranges from 14% to 70%.

Mehta's CLEAR framework (arXiv 2511.14136, 2025) introduces Cost-Normalized Accuracy (CNA = Accuracy/Cost × 100) and Cost Per Success (CPS), and on 300 enterprise tasks finds 'accuracy-optimal configurations cost 4.4–10.8× more than Pareto-efficient alternatives' and 50× cost variations across agents at similar accuracy, with Reflexion at $5.12/task being dominated by Plan-Execute at $1.24/task with comparable efficacy.

The financial-document benchmark (Kulkarni & Kulkarni, 2025) shows the reflexive multi-agent architecture achieves the highest F1 of 0.943 but at 2.3× sequential baseline cost; the hierarchical architecture achieves 98.5% of that F1 at 60.7% of the cost; and a 'Hierarchical-Optimized' configuration combining caching+routing+adaptive retry recovers 89% of reflexive's accuracy gain at only 1.15× sequential baseline cost, demonstrating that cost normalization can move quality gaps from dominant to negligible.

The same financial benchmark shows reflexive multi-agent has p99/p50 latency ratio of 3.34× (vs 1.6× for sequential), and BECOMES the worst-performing architecture above 50K docs/day under fixed compute because timeout-truncated correction loops eliminate its accuracy advantage; the architectural crossover where hierarchical drops below parallel occurs around 75K docs/day.

BATS / Budget-Aware Test-time Scaling (Liu et al., Google Cloud AI Research, November 2025) formalizes a unified cost metric combining token cost and tool-call cost, and shows that without explicit budget awareness, ReAct-style agents saturate (~12% on BrowseComp) regardless of how much additional budget is allocated; budget-aware planning + verification produces a substantially better Pareto curve (24.6% on BrowseComp vs 12.6% for vanilla ReAct on Gemini-2.5-Pro at the same 100-tool-call budget).

BAMAS (Yang et al., November 2025) demonstrates that constructing budget-constrained MAS via Integer Linear Programming for LLM selection plus reinforcement learning for topology selection can achieve comparable accuracy to AutoGen, MetaGPT, and ChatDev at up to 86% lower cost — directly evidencing that the 'multi-agent' label is largely an over-spec that can be tuned cost-down without quality loss.

Tran & Kiela document a critical methodological pitfall in token-based normalization: Gemini-2.5's API-reported `thoughts_token_count` is up to 4.7× the visible-thought token count, and SAS visible thought plateaus at ~350 tokens regardless of the requested 1k–10k budget, while Sequential MAS naturally surfaces more visible-thought text by concatenating k agent calls — meaning naive token comparisons systematically favor MAS for spurious reasons.

The community recommendation emerging from this literature is multi-axis Pareto reporting: leaderboards should publish accuracy alongside input/output token counts, tool-call counts, dollar cost at a stated date, and wall-clock p50/p95/p99, and present rankings as Pareto frontiers; Kapoor et al. and Mehta provide reference implementations, but deep-research benchmarks (LiveResearchBench, DeepResearch Bench) have not yet adopted this — BrowseComp-Plus is the leading exception.

On the question of when MAS does win: Tran & Kiela's degradation experiments show MAS becomes competitive only when single-agent context utilization is heavily degraded (e.g., 70% token substitution); Kim et al. (2025), cited in the same paper, find that under matched compute, agentic MAS benefits 'tend to concentrate in weaker model or harder-regime settings and diminish (or even reverse) as base model capability increases.'

disagreements: Anthropic frames multi-agent systems as genuinely valuable when 'the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance' and reports a 90.2% improvement of multi-agent over single-agent Claude Opus 4 on internal research evals, while Tran & Kiela and Kim et al. argue most such gains evaporate under matched-token comparison, with Kim et al. specifically finding agentic benefits 'diminish (or even reverse) as base model capability increases.' Anthropic partially concedes the point by reporting that 80% of variance is explained by token usage alone — the disagreement is therefore as much about framing (architecture vs compute attribution) as about the underlying numbers.

There is no consensus on the 'right' compute-cost metric: Kapoor et al. argue dollars (with raw token counts also reported), Tran & Kiela use thinking-token budgets specifically, BATS uses a unified token-cost + tool-call-cost metric, AgentTTS uses FLOPs, and Mehta's CLEAR uses dollars combined with latency, assurance, and reliability into a composite. None of these have been adopted by the major deep-research benchmarks (LiveResearchBench, DeepResearch Bench).

Tran & Kiela document that token-based normalization is itself non-trivial because API-reported token counts can be inflated by 4.7× for Gemini and Sequential MAS naturally surfaces more visible thought tokens by concatenation; they recommend comparing on the *requested* budget, but this is not yet standard.

LiveResearchBench v5 reports multi-agent systems leading on average composite scores (Open Deep Research with GPT-5: 73.7) and on citation/presentation, but on Analysis Depth most systems lose to a strong baseline — only Deerflow+ and Gemini Deep Research win on depth — illustrating that quality 'gaps' depend strongly on which dimension is averaged. Without cost normalization, this aggregation choice itself produces conflicting MAS-vs-SAS rankings.

findings.sub_question: What architectural choices have enterprise / regulated-industry deep-research deployments (legal, medical, financial, scientific literature review) actually adopted in 2024–2026, and what do their published case studies reveal about which trade-offs (auditability, citation faithfulness, latency, cost, prompt-injection blast radius) dominated their single- vs multi-agent decision?
findings.summary:
Across the four regulated domains surveyed, enterprise deep-research deployments in 2024–2026 have converged on an architecturally similar pattern but make domain-specific trade-offs that drive the single- vs multi-agent decision. The dominant pattern is what Thomson Reuters calls a 'three-dials' design (autonomy, tools/context, memory/coordination) implemented as a hierarchical orchestrator + specialized worker agents with a hard generation-verification loop, model-agnostic backends, schema-first / structured outputs, and curated rather than open-web corpora. Salesforce EDR, ServiceNow EDRA, Thomson Reuters CoCounsel/Westlaw Deep Research, Medable's Agent Studio, and Carnegie Mellon's Medical Deep Research all explicitly orchestrate specialized retrieval/reasoning sub-agents around a master planner with reflection, while LITERAS (medicine) and LiRA (scientific lit-review) use the same template at smaller scale.

In the legal domain, the binding constraint is citation faithfulness and audit defensibility, not latency. Thomson Reuters Deep Research (live August 2025; CoCounsel reimagined April 2026 on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK) deliberately runs ~10 minutes (with 3-, 7-, and forthcoming 20-minute tiers) against a curated 20B+ document Westlaw corpus, never the open web. They explicitly chose multi-agent specialization by document type (case law / statutes / secondary sources), and built a 'patent-pending citation ledger' so the agent can only cite what it actually retrieved. The cost is opaque but the team accepts it; 'defensibility is the whole point.' In finance, the binding constraint is determinism / replayability for SR 11-7-style audits, which inverts some assumptions: Khatchadourian's 2026 IBM-published Determinism-Faithfulness Assurance Harness (DFAH) showed 7–20B-parameter Tier 1 models with schema-first architectures achieved 100% trajectory determinism, while 120B+ models dropped to 9.7% and required 3.7× more validation samples. Multi-agent tool-use reintroduced variance, leading the author to recommend Tier 1 + schema-first for AML/compliance triage and reserving frontier multi-agent stacks for human-in-the-loop advisory. The Kulkarni SEC-filing benchmark (10K filings, 4 architectures × 5 models) reached the same Pareto conclusion: hierarchical supervisor-worker dominated (F1 0.929 at $0.261/doc, 60.7% of reflexive cost), while the most-accurate reflexive multi-agent (F1 0.943) degraded fastest under load — at >50K docs/day it became the worst-performing architecture as queueing-induced timeouts truncated correction loops. Chen et al.'s ICML 2025 M-SAEA framework formalized the new failure modes that only emerge in multi-agent finance deployments — temporal staleness, cross-agent race conditions, optimistic trust between peers, and prompt-injection blast radius spreading through inter-agent messages — with documented incidents (Freysa AI agent's $47K loss; ChatGPT-recommended phishing site costing a user $2,500).

In medicine, the trade-off is between citation grounding and clinical actionability. OpenEvidence (Mayo Clinic Platform Accelerate–developed, used by ~40% of U.S. physicians by late 2025) is essentially a single-agent retrieval-grounded LLM pinned to peer-reviewed JAMA/NEJM/society guidelines; Mayo's own evaluation found it scored 3.6/4 on satisfaction but only 1.95/4 on impact-on-decision because it primarily reinforces existing plans. Multi-agent alternatives explicitly target this gap: LITERAS (Computers in Biology and Medicine 2025) uses an iterative Critic Agent loop and reaches 99.82% citation correctness against Sonar/Sonar-Pro baselines; CMU's Medical Deep Research (NeurIPS 2025 GenAI for Health workshop) and Shanghai Jiao Tong's Deep-DxSearch (Aug 2025/Feb 2026) use multi-agent RL with explicit retrieval traces, with Deep-DxSearch raising physician diagnostic accuracy from 45.6% to 69.1% but receiving lower time-efficiency scores (2.0 vs 4.0 for DeepSeek-R1) — clinicians explicitly accepted the latency penalty for auditable evidence chains. Medable's Agent Studio (2026) and DeepER-Med (April 2026) make the same trade explicit, framing the workflow as 'inspectable' and 'evidence-based.'

In scientific literature review, deployed systems split into two camps. Single-agent or fixed-pipeline tools (OpenEvidence, early Undermind, Elicit) emphasize speed and predictability but were shown by Salesforce's DeepTRACE audit (Sept 2025) to have 40–80% citation accuracy and 12–97% unsupported-statement rates — even in 'deep research' mode, 54–94% of debate-query answers were one-sided. The newer multi-agent systems (Salesforce EDR, ServiceNow EDRA, LiRA, Purdue's Elhuyar, LANL's URSA, Undermind Projects) explicitly add real-time human steering, todo.md state, and reflection loops to address these failure modes, accepting roughly 4× higher token cost than single-agent baselines (EDR uses 53.9M tokens at $117 per DeepResearch Bench run) in exchange for citation accuracy and steerability. A consistent observation from practitioners (Aaron Tay's April 2026 analysis) is that multi-agent agentic systems introduce a new usability problem — the 'invisible menu problem' — where users cannot discover what the system can do, which compounds the auditability problem because the agent's tool selections are not visible.

Across all four domains, the dominant trade-off was NOT cost vs accuracy but auditability/faithfulness vs latency-and-cost. Multi-agent specialization won wherever (a) different document types or sub-questions required heterogeneous expertise (Thomson Reuters, Medable, EDR, LITERAS) or (b) verification could be isolated as a dedicated agent (the generation-verification loop appears in essentially every regulated deployment). Single-agent architectures held on where determinism/replayability was the binding constraint (financial compliance triage per DFAH, regulatory reporting), where latency was paramount (point-of-care clinical Q&A à la OpenEvidence), or where the prompt-injection blast radius of multi-agent inter-agent message passing could not be acceptably bounded (M-SAEA's documented cross-agent-cascade vulnerabilities). Frontier-model multi-agent stacks were universally relegated to human-in-the-loop advisory rather than autonomous decision paths.

key_facts.claim: Thomson Reuters' Deep Research in Westlaw/CoCounsel went live August 2025 with a multi-agent architecture using specialized document-type agents (case law, statutes, secondary sources) orchestrated around a master planner; the system runs ~10 minutes against a curated 20-billion-document Westlaw corpus (not the open web), with 3-, 7-, and 10-minute tiers and a forthcoming 20-minute version.

Thomson Reuters explicitly traded latency for depth: lawyers preferred longer-running outputs and the team has stated they are 'comfortable making it slower' to improve quality; they emphasize that 'defensibility is the whole point' and built a patent-pending citation-ledger architecture to ensure the agent can only cite what it actually retrieved.

Thomson Reuters' next-generation CoCounsel Legal (April 2026 beta) is built on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK as a unified agentic platform with Westlaw and Practical Law content natively embedded, evaluated by practicing-attorney editors who define correct outputs before any capability ships.

Salesforce's Enterprise Deep Research (EDR, October 2025) uses a multi-agent architecture with a Master Planning Agent, four specialized search agents (General, Academic, GitHub, LinkedIn), an MCP-based tool ecosystem, and a todo.md-driven steerable reflection mechanism; it achieved 50.6 (49.86 reported elsewhere) on DeepResearch Bench at ~53.9M tokens and $117 per run, outperforming OpenAI Deep Research, Gemini Deep Research, and Claude Research.

ServiceNow's EDRA (November 2025) is explicitly designed as a 'privacy-aware' multi-agent system for enterprise research over confidential data, achieving 67.2% on the DRBench enterprise benchmark using hundreds of action and reasoning steps.

On a 10,000-SEC-filing benchmark across 4 architectures and 5 models, hierarchical supervisor-worker multi-agent architectures occupied the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier (F1 0.929 at $0.261/doc), while reflexive self-correcting multi-agent reached the highest accuracy (F1 0.943) at 2.3× sequential cost; reflexive architectures degraded fastest at scale, becoming the worst performer above 50K documents/day due to queuing-induced timeout truncation of correction loops.

An IBM-published Determinism-Faithfulness Assurance Harness (DFAH, January 2026) found that 7–20B-parameter Tier 1 models with schema-first architectures achieved 100% trajectory determinism on financial compliance triage, while 120B+ Tier 3 models reached only 9.7% determinism and required 3.7× larger validation samples; the author recommends Tier 1 + schema-first for AML/compliance and reserving frontier models for human-in-the-loop advisory only.

DFAH explicitly distinguishes pass@k (one-of-k success) from pass^k (all-of-k success) and argues compliance audits require pass^k determinism — every flagged decision must reproduce identically — which favors smaller deterministic single-agent stacks over frontier multi-agent stacks where API-level non-determinism persists.

The ICML 2025 M-SAEA framework documented that multi-agent financial deployments introduce failure modes invisible to single-agent evaluation, including cross-agent cascade risk, optimistic trust between peers (each treats peer messages as ground truth), race conditions on shared trading APIs, and a wider prompt-injection blast radius; cited real incidents include the Freysa AI agent losing $47,000 to prompt-injection and a ChatGPT-recommended phishing site costing a user $2,500.

OpenEvidence is the dominant single-agent medical deep-research tool (used by ~40% of U.S. physicians by late 2025), developed via the Mayo Clinic Platform Accelerate program and partnered with Elsevier ClinicalKey; in a Mayo Clinic primary-care evaluation across 5 chronic-disease cases it scored 3.6/4 on satisfaction but only 1.95/4 on impact on clinical decision-making, primarily reinforcing rather than modifying physician plans.

LITERAS (Computers in Biology and Medicine 2025) is a multi-agent biomedical literature-review system using an iterative Critic Agent loop that achieved 99.82% citation correctness, exclusively cited Q1–Q2 peer-reviewed journals, and outperformed Sonar/Sonar-Pro on academic-source retrieval; the multi-agent iterative approach was credited with minimizing hallucinations.

Carnegie Mellon's Medical Deep Research (NeurIPS 2025 GenAI for Health workshop) uses a LangGraph multi-agent architecture (Coordinator/Planner/Orchestrator/Researcher/Coder/Reporter) with curated medical resources plus a dynamic MCP integration pipeline that automatically discovers, validates, and integrates new MCP servers; expert review found 0% hallucinated references across cases and average correctness/helpfulness of 4.8/5.

Shanghai Jiao Tong/Xinhua Hospital's Deep-DxSearch (Aug 2025/Feb 2026) is an end-to-end RL-trained agentic RAG system that improved physician diagnostic accuracy from 45.6% (unaided) to 69.1% (assisted) on 150 real-world cases, but explicitly accepted a latency penalty: clinicians scored it lower on time efficiency (2.0 vs 4.0 for DeepSeek-R1) while strongly preferring its auditable evidence-chain over R1's opaque chain-of-thought (reasoning-transparency 4.2 vs 3.3).

Salesforce's DeepTRACE audit framework (September 2025) found that public deep-research agents (GPT-5 DR, YouChat DR, Perplexity DR, Copilot Think Deeper, Gemini DR) had citation accuracy of 40–80%, unsupported-statement rates of 12.5–97.5%, and one-sidedness on debate queries of 54.7–94.8%, demonstrating that multi-step multi-agent retrieval does not automatically deliver citation faithfulness.

DeepER-Med (April 2026) frames medical deep research as an explicit, inspectable three-module workflow (research planning, agentic collaboration, evidence synthesis), arguing that existing systems lack 'explicit and inspectable criteria for evidence appraisal' creating 'risk of compounding errors' — a critique that drives regulated-industry deployments toward decomposed multi-agent architectures with externalized state.

Medable's Agent Studio (2026) deploys configurable multi-agent systems for clinical trial operations, processing 80,000+ documents/year and monitoring data across 13+ disparate systems, using model-agnostic agents, RAG knowledge integration, MCP connectors, and robust evaluation frameworks aimed at reducing trial timelines from 10 years to 1 year.

Snorkel's 2025 insurance underwriting benchmark (developed with Chartered Property and Casualty Underwriters) found tool-use failures in 36% of multi-agent conversations and that OpenAI models hallucinated non-existent insurance products in 15–45% of conversations, with frontier-model accuracy ranging from single digits to ~80%, illustrating that multi-agent capability gains in regulated-finance settings are uneven and accompanied by new failure modes.

LiRA (October 2025) is a four-agent literature-review system (outline, write, edit, review) that outperformed AutoSurvey and MASS-Survey on SciReviewGen and a proprietary ScienceDirect dataset, demonstrating that the multi-agent template extends down to scientific literature review even without domain-specific tuning.

Aaron Tay's April 2026 hands-on analysis of agentic academic search (Elicit Research Agents, Undermind Projects, SciSpace Agents) identifies an 'invisible menu' usability problem specific to agentic deployments: when systems can theoretically do anything, users cannot discover what they actually do, which directly damages reproducibility and trust because tool invocations and alternative paths are not visible — a concrete cost of moving from fixed pipelines to multi-agent flexibility.

Across legal (Thomson Reuters), enterprise (Salesforce EDR, ServiceNow EDRA), and medical (CMU Medical Deep Research, DeepER-Med, Medable) deployments, deployed multi-agent systems converge on a near-identical template: master/orchestrator agent + specialized worker/retrieval agents + dedicated verification or critic agent + externalized state (e.g., todo.md) + human-in-the-loop steering + curated rather than open-web corpora.

In every regulated-industry deployment surveyed, generation-verification (or generation-critic) loops are treated as essential, and citation grounding is implemented as a system primitive (citation ledger at Thomson Reuters; ICS confidence scoring + journal-credibility pipeline in CMU Medical Deep Research; iterative Critic Agent in LITERAS; evidence-grounding heuristic in DFAH) rather than as post-hoc fact-checking.
